final_proof:
Let $f(t)$ be expressed in its real and imaginary parts as:
$$f(t) = u(t) + i v(t)$$
where $u, v: [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ are continuous real-valued functions.

By the definition of the definite integral of a complex-valued function, we evaluate the integrals over the intervals $[a, c]$ and $[c, b]$ by integrating their real and imaginary parts separately:
$$\int_a^c f(t) dt = \int_a^c u(t) dt + i \int_a^c v(t) dt$$
$$\int_c^b f(t) dt = \int_c^b u(t) dt + i \int_c^b v(t) dt$$

Adding these two equations, we can group the real and imaginary components:
$$\int_a^c f(t) dt + \int_c^b f(t) dt = \left( \int_a^c u(t) dt + \int_c^b u(t) dt \right) + i \left( \int_a^c v(t) dt + \int_c^b v(t) dt \right)$$

For continuous real-valued functions, the sum of integrals over adjacent intervals $[a, c]$ and $[c, b]$ is equal to the integral over the combined interval $[a, b]$. Therefore:
$$\int_a^c u(t) dt + \int_c^b u(t) dt = \int_a^b u(t) dt$$
$$\int_a^c v(t) dt + \int_c^b v(t) dt = \int_a^b v(t) dt$$

Substituting these results back into our grouped equation yields:
$$\int_a^c f(t) dt + \int_c^b f(t) dt = \int_a^b u(t) dt + i \int_a^b v(t) dt$$

By the definition of the definite integral of a complex function, the right-hand side is exactly the integral of $f(t)$ over $[a, b]$:
$$\int_a^b u(t) dt + i \int_a^b v(t) dt = \int_a^b f(t) dt$$

Hence, we conclude that:
$$\int_a^c f(t) dt + \int_c^b f(t) dt = \int_a^b f(t) dt$$
This completes the proof.
